Chapter Three—Getting Stuck: The Cost of Clinging to the Past.
So, picture this—when the cheese disappeared, everything changed for the little people. Their world was flipped upside down. And suddenly, it wasn’t just about missing the cheese. It was about losing their sense of security. One of them, especially, just couldn’t let go. Day after day, he kept returning to that empty spot, hoping things would somehow go back to normal. You can imagine the frustration building up—he grew resentful, even convinced that someone had stolen what was his.
Sound familiar? Honestly, a lot of us react this way when life throws us a curveball. We fall into old habits, clinging to what once worked, hoping that if we just wait it out, everything will magically return to how it used to be. The comfort of the past becomes this invisible trap, making it almost impossible to spot new possibilities.
Now, the other little person? He struggled, too, but after wrestling with his thoughts, he started to wonder—maybe waiting isn’t the answer. The longer he hung around, the more anxious and powerless he felt. That maze, which used to be full of adventure, suddenly felt more like a prison. Sure, the idea of heading out into the unknown was scary. But honestly, staying put was starting to hurt even more.
Meanwhile, the mice? They didn’t sit around blaming or overthinking. They just noticed the change, accepted it, and got moving. Their approach was refreshingly simple: spot change early, adapt fast, and keep exploring.
For the little people, though, leaving behind the old cheese was terrifying. What if there wasn’t anything better out there? What if the maze was too risky? These doubts kept them stuck, even as their situation became more and more uncomfortable.
Here’s what really stands out: holding on to the past, no matter how safe it feels, can actually keep you from discovering new opportunities. The longer they waited for things to return to normal, the clearer it became—life wasn’t going to change back just for them. If they wanted things to improve, they’d have to be the ones to change.
